newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS--Italian July car market leaps,orders steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Italian July car market leaps,orders steady.

text.p: Italy's new car market showed a further surge in July rising 54.06 percent from year ago levels, and many car dealers see new vehicle deliveries holding steady over the next three to four months.

Italian Transport Minister figures on Friday showed July new car registrations leap to 246,500 from 160,007 in July 1996, with Italy's carmaker Fiat outperforming the market with its July deliveries up 57.13 percent to 108,970.

Sharp rises this year have been fuelled by Italy's new car incentive buying scheme, which has recently been extended for a further 10 months. June deliveries were up 50.71 percent with Fiat then again outperforming the market, up 65.8 percent.

The buying scheme started in January, and funded by the government and car industry, offers price discounts to owners of cars of over 10 years old that trade them in for scrapping when they purchase a new car.

In the seven month period January-July the scheme has been operating, new car registrations in Italy have risen 34.40 percent to 1,558,900 vehicles. In this same period, Fiat group new registrations have increased 32.6 percent to 676,651.

The strong recovery in Italian domestic car production has helped drive up Italy's industrial production with data today showing June national output up 1.3 percent year-on-year after adjusting for an extra working day in June 1997.
National Statistics Institute ISTAT said that higher car production in June, with transport output up 16.2 percent year-on-year, had helped boost overall industrial production.
Car research body Centro Studi Promotor (CSP) said orders for new cars showed a moderate rise in July over June and expectations for the next quarter saw deliveries holding steady.

In its regular survey of car dealers, CSP said the number seeing high levels of orders had risen in June and added half the new cars ordered benefited from the scheme. Some 55 percent saw deliveries holding steady in the next three to four months.
Italy recently extended the scheme from its planned close at end-September until end-July but reduced cash incentives and moved to encourage the buying of more fuel efficient cars.

Car industry analysts said the scheme would continue to help the car market, but were concerned over the size of a possible slump when the scheme finally finished next year, and the effect the scheme would have on car manufacturers' margins.
"The scheme helps consumers and benefts the environment, but does little to help industry profit margins," said one analyst.

Industry sources said the Fiat group, which also takes in car marques Alfa Romeo and Lancia, saw its share of the European car market hold steady at 13 percent in July in line with June, and up from 11.9 percent in July 1996.

In the seven month period January-July, the group saw its European share at 12.6 percent from 11.8 percent in the same period of 1996. This confirmed Fiat in second place in the European car industry behind German group Volkswagen.
